short: William Tyndale was a leading figure in the Protestant Reformation who translated the Bible into English from the original Greek and Hebrew.
full:
Frustrated by the Church's ban on unauthorized English Bibles, William Tyndale moved to mainland Europe to translate the scriptures directly from the original Greek and Hebrew, rather than relying on the Latin Vulgate. His New Testament, first printed in 1526, heavily influenced subsequent English Bibles. Many of his phrases, such as "let there be light" and "the powers that be," became permanent fixtures of the English language.

Tyndale's work was fiercely opposed by the English establishment, particularly Thomas More, who viewed his translations and Protestant theological notes as heretical. Hunted across Europe by agents of Henry VIII and the Holy Roman Emperor, Tyndale was eventually betrayed in Antwerp. He was strangled and burned at the stake in 1536, reportedly crying out, "Lord! Open the King of England's eyes!"
